opening.headline: You have company policies, but how do you know if your admin console settings follow them?
body: Company regulations include prohibition on unauthorized external integration and restrictions on the use of some functions in sensitive departments. However, the Administrator console is littered with feature switches, roles, groups, and user synchronization settings. Without knowing how rule sentences and console entries flow together, a rule becomes nothing more than a declaration.

In this class, the administrator consoles of the three products are organized into three axes: who, what function, and by what unit. Next, we will check how to adapt the approach to changes in people using rules for adding roles, inheritance rules, SSO and SCIM, and explain cases where new features are deployed by default.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain administrator settings and access control by function
Control items can be distinguished by function and user group.

screens.title: There are regulations, but I don't know if they are followed.
screens.lead: Read the situations below and think about what more is needed to make the rules stick in reality.

visual.alt: Illustration of two regulatory statements and four settings items in the administrator console connected by broken arrows.

paragraphs: Company regulations state that unauthorized external integration is prohibited. There is also a sentence stating that sensitive departments restrict the use of some features. If you just read the regulations, it looks like it's under control.

However, when I open the Administrator Console, feature switches, roles, groups, and user synchronization settings are scattered across several screens. Many organizations operate without knowing which setting items the regulatory sentences correspond to. For regulations to be followed in reality, they must be translated into configuration items.
This class covers how to read administrator settings based on product documentation and match regulations to setting items.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When a new AI feature is released, will it be on or off in our organization? See why defaults are important in the commentary.

screens.outro: First, let's recall your experience dealing with the Administrator Console.

screens.title: Have you ever tried turning features off and on in the administrator console?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. Since you will not submit an answer, first think about our organization.

items.prompt: When a new AI feature came out, was it on or off in my organization?
items.answer: Each product has different default values, and if you don't know the default values, your employees may find out about them first. Some products are shipped with the feature turned on, so you need to take steps to check the default for each new feature.

items.prompt: Have different departments ever needed different access to a feature?
items.answer: Batch transcription settings have limitations. There is a way to set it up by dividing it into roles, groups, or organizational units. In the demonstration, we will check which units exist for each product.

items.prompt: Have you ever checked whether the access rights of employees who left the company are automatically organized?
items.answer: Depending on how the user syncs, they may be automatically removed, or the list and seats may remain. If you are not aware of this difference, you may end up leaving an account for a retired employee.

screens.outro: Let's take a closer look at how units are divided and the rules for roles and groups.

screens.title: Role-based access and group settings
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to read the rules by role and group one by one. It's good to pay attention to how permissions are combined and which settings override which.

steps.title: OpenAI: Power adds up
steps.body: In an OpenAI workspace, users can have multiple roles and roles through groups. The permissions of general roles are additive, so if any of the assigned roles is granted, the user maintains access. This applies to both directly assigned roles and roles assigned to groups.

steps.title: OpenAI: Three States
steps.body: A role's permissions have three states: Default, On, and Off. Default inherits workspace settings. Access is denied only when all relevant roles are Off, so even if set to Off, access may be maintained because other roles are turned on.

steps.title: OpenAI: Lockdown Mode
steps.body: Lockdown Mode is evaluated separately and may restrict functionality even if normal roles allow it. Seat type, plan, and product eligibility still apply. So, when access is not possible, you should look at these three things together rather than just looking at the role settings.

steps.title: Google: Organizational units and groups
steps.body: Google Workspace divides its audience into organizational units (OUs). OU is often used to represent a department. This can also be applied to configuration groups in an advanced way, where the group settings override the OU settings. If your settings are not what you expected, check which unit won.

steps.title: Google: Queries through other apps
steps.body: The document warns that even if you turn off the Gemini feature in one app, other apps can still use Gemini and query that app's data. For example, even if you turn off Gmail, other apps may ask for your Gmail data. Function control does not end with turning on and off each service, but also requires checking bypass routes.

screens.outro: Now that you know the rules of authority, let's look at how to adapt your approach to people's fluctuations.

screens.title: SSO and SCIM: Adapting approaches to human variation
screens.lead: Click the toggle to compare how JIT and SCIM differ in how they account for people changes, such as departures or transfers.

states.label: JIT provisioning
states.body: Claude chooses a provisioning method after SSO. Invitation only is standard, and there is JIT and SCIM directory synchronization. JIT is a method created when a user assigned to an IdP app logs in for the first time, and can be used in all plans. However, the JIT does not automatically remove users. Unassigning from the IdP will prevent logins, but user lists and seats will remain until cleared by an administrator. If you delete it only from Claude, it may be added again at the next SSO login, so if you want to remove it permanently, it must be processed by both Claude and the IdP.

states.label: SCIM synchronization
states.body: SCIM automatically creates users based on their IdP assignment, even before logging in, and automatically deletes them when they are removed from the IdP. Claude supports only Enterprise and Console organizations and cannot be used in Team plans. OpenAI's SCIM is also used in Enterprise and Edu workspaces, and is not included in the Business exclusive plan. If a role is linked to a group, permission changes due to movement and removal due to leaving the company will automatically follow. Therefore, in organizations where organizing access to employees who have left the company is important, whether the plan is capable of SCIM is a selection criterion.

screens.outro: Now, let's explain an example of a new feature being deployed by default.

screens.title: Commentary: When a new feature is deployed as turned on by default
screens.lead: This is an example where a vendor has released a new AI feature and the default is on. Follow the five-step response sequence.

steps.title: Organize the case
steps.body: A vendor comes out with a new AI feature. In products that are turned on by default, such as the Gemini feature in Google Workspace, employees can use the feature without administrators having to do anything. The regulations require it to be turned on after approval, but the default is ahead of the regulations.

steps.title: Step 1: Check the defaults
steps.body: Check the documentation for product-specific defaults. OpenAI first looks at the workspace default values ​​of Permissions & roles and the status of each role (Default, On, Off). In addition to the defaults, check whether the role inherits or whether other roles have it turned on.

steps.title: Step 2: Look at your scope of influence
steps.body: Determine which service and which organizational unit applies. Google looks at whether it's turned on for each service and which OUs and groups it applies to. If you don't know the scope of influence, you can't determine the extent to which it will be turned off.

steps.title: Step 3: Check against policy
steps.body: Compare the current state with the default state required by regulation: off or on after approval. If the corresponding function is not in the regulations, decide whether to change the regulations or turn off the function.

steps.title: Step 4: Turn it on only where needed
steps.body: Turn on the feature only for groups that need it, such as organizational units or roles. Make sure that group settings do not overwrite OU settings and add role permissions, leaving them open to unintended users.

steps.title: Step 5: Write it down
steps.body: Record the changes made to the settings and the rationale. Documenting the function, status before and after the change, supporting documentation, who made the change, and the date will help show compliance with regulations and settings during an audit.

screens.outro: Let's see how to turn this commentary into repeatable operating rules.

screens.title: Commentary: Checking default values as operating rules
screens.lead: When you select an item, the content and reasons for the operating rules will unfold. It is the process of turning a one-time response into a sustainable inspection.

items.prompt: What columns should I put in the feature list?
items.answer: Leave the following columns: Product, Default, State as required by regulation, Settlor, and Confirmed Date. Checking becomes easier if you prioritize rows that have different states from the default values ​​and regulations.

items.prompt: When do we put new features on the checklist?
items.answer: Raise it before turning it on. For features that are already enabled and deployed, we'll upload them as soon as we know they're available and check their scope of impact. You need to set a uploader and a deadline to keep it. For example, decide who will receive release notifications and decide whether to check the default value within a few business days.

items.prompt: It's turned on, but what do I do with functions that aren't in the regulations?
items.answer: Fix rules or turn off features. If the regulations and settings are left out of sync, the regulations become nothing more than declarations, so be sure to change one of the two to make it match. Which one to change is decided based on whether the function is necessary for the job and what the risks are.

items.prompt: How to check the detour route
items.answer: Check whether the feature turned off in one app is used by another app. That's because, as Google Docs warns, even if you turn it off in one app, other apps can query that app's data. During the inspection, connections between major apps are also viewed. The inspection results are recorded in the Verification Date column of the function list for comparison during the next inspection. Repeat this check quarterly and whenever there is a major product change.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the operating rules, let's gather the key points.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Features are determined by policy, not by default
screens.lead: Summarizes the contents of this class.

paragraphs: Control items in the console are organized into three axes: who, what function, and by what unit. Role permissions are additive and default values ​​are inherited, and in some products group settings override organizational unit settings. SSO and SCIM are means of organizing access as people fluctuate.

Default values for new features vary by product, so check them first. Write the default value and the status required by the regulation side by side in the function list. Write the default value and the status required by the regulation side by side in the function list, add the person in charge and the confirmation date, and adjust the misaligned fields to one of the regulations or settings. Also check if features turned off in one app are bypassed by other apps. Record inspection results with date so they can be compared during the next inspection.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Rules must be translated into console entries to be followed.

checks.intro: Check the rules for aggregating role permissions yourself. This confirmation is not logged.
checks.q: In an OpenAI workspace, what happens to access when one role of a user has a feature Off and another role has it On?
options: Access is possible because permissions are added.
Off takes priority and access is blocked.
checks.explain: The permissions of multiple roles are added, and access is possible if any one is granted permission. Lockdown Mode is evaluated separately.

wrong.1: Off does not take precedence. Allowing even one will ensure access is maintained.
wrong.2: Follow permission aggregation rules, not granting order.
wrong.3: Default inheritance is the rule when in the Default state.

checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. Permissions are additive, so if you grant one, access is maintained.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's easy to think that Off prevents everything, but that's not the rule. Think again about how authority is combined.

checks.intro: Match features with provisioning methods. For each method on the left, choose an appropriate explanation from the right.
checks.q: Pair these features with the following provisioning methods:
right: Users are created on first login, but are not automatically removed when deleted from the IdP
Automatically creates and deletes users based on IdP assignment
The default method is that only the people you invite can create an account.
Permissions are automatically organized upon resignation or transfer.
checks.explain: The provisioning method determines the extent to which changes in people are reflected in access.
checks.correctFeedback: All four methods were connected appropriately. It was pointed out that whether or not it is automatically removed determines the method.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some connections are off. Divide them again based on when users are created and how they are deleted.

glossary.def: This is a console item that sets feature availability and policies at an organizational level.
This is a method of assigning roles to users and controlling access to functions using the roles.
A single authentication method that logs in with your organization's IdP.
A provisioning standard that automatically creates and clears accounts based on user assignments from the IdP.
Whether the feature is turned on when not specified by the administrator.

misconceptions.myth: If you create regulations, the settings also follow.
misconceptions.fact: You must translate the rules into console items and set them to ensure they are followed.

misconceptions.myth: If you turn off the function, bypass is impossible.
misconceptions.fact: Even if you turn it off in one app, other apps can query that app's data, the document warns.

misconceptions.myth: If you delete a user from the IdP, all access is cleared.
misconceptions.fact: JIT leaves behind a list of users and seats. Automatic removal takes place in SCIM.

closing.lead: We recapitulate the key points of this lesson.
points: Control items are organized by who, what function, and by what unit.
Role permissions are additive and default values are inherited.
For new features, check the default values first.
